# Sendr

> Sendr is an email tool a person deploys to their own Cloudflare account. It sends campaigns and single emails through their Amazon SES account, and an agent runs it through its API.

The user gave you this link to set Sendr up. Work through the steps in order, running the commands yourself. Each step ends with a check; meet it before you start the next one. Ask the user only for decisions, facts about their business, and approvals.

## 1. Look for an existing instance

List `~/.config/sendr/`. Each `<host>.env` file there is a Sendr instance this machine set up before. If you find one, ask whether the user wants to use it or deploy a new instance for another project (one instance holds one project's contacts). To use an existing one, install the skill from step 9 if it's missing, then follow the skill instead of this guide.

Done when you know you're deploying a new instance.

## 2. Introduce Sendr

Tell the user briefly, in your own words, what they're about to get:

- Their own email tool, running in their Cloudflare account as one Worker with a D1 database, a queue and an R2 bucket for images and video. Contacts, unsubscribes and stats stay with them. It costs almost nothing to run, and SES charges about $0.10 per 1,000 emails.
- Campaigns written in a rich editor with images, GIFs, and video and audio cards, or in their own HTML or plain text. Merge tags like `{{first_name|there}}`, a live preview in light and dark, and a footer shared by every campaign. Each campaign goes to a first batch of 200 people, then waits for approval before the rest.
- Every campaign has a visible unsubscribe link and the one-click unsubscribe button Gmail and Apple Mail show. Addresses that bounced or reported spam never get mail again.
- Stats for each campaign: delivered, bounced, complained, opened, and clicks per link.
- Single emails, like receipts and welcome notes, sent from their app through the same API.
- An API for everything. Their app syncs contacts, and you manage campaigns, senders and settings, and show them a picture of each campaign before it goes out. There's also an admin app with passkey sign-in, for when they want to look themselves.

Then list what you need from step 3, and wait for their go-ahead.

Done when the user agrees to go ahead.

## 3. Get access

You need:

- Cloudflare, to deploy. Check with `bunx wrangler whoami`. If Wrangler isn't signed in, run `bunx wrangler login`, which opens a browser for the user.
- Cloudflare DNS, to verify the sending domain. Wrangler's login can't edit DNS. If the sending domain is on Cloudflare, ask the user to connect Cloudflare's API MCP server (`https://mcp.cloudflare.com/mcp`) or give you an API token with Zone > DNS > Edit for that zone. Without either, the user adds the records at their DNS host from the list you give them.
- AWS, to set up SES. Check with `aws sts get-caller-identity`. You need the account that will send, with rights to create IAM users and manage SES. An AWS MCP server that runs IAM and SES calls works too. A user with no AWS account creates one at https://aws.amazon.com first.
- `git` and `bun` (https://bun.sh).

Ask the user for:

- Their email. They sign in to Sendr with it, and nobody else can.
- Sendr's own address, a subdomain of a domain in their Cloudflare account, like `emails.acme.com`. Unsubscribe links use it, so pick one they'll keep. If none of their domains are on Cloudflare, Sendr runs on the `workers.dev` address Wrangler gives it.
- The From name and address, like `Acme <news@acme.com>`, and an AWS region near their users (`us-east-1` if they don't mind).
- Their company name and postal address for the footer. Anti-spam laws require an address.
- Where to keep the Sendr checkout. Updates deploy from it.
- Their app's repository, if they have one. The Sendr skill goes there in step 9.
- Whether their Cloudflare account has Workers Paid, the $5 a month plan. Wrangler can't show the plan, so ask. They can see it on the Workers plans page in the Cloudflare dashboard.

If the account is on Workers Free, or they aren't sure, tell them what Free allows, in plain words: "Workers Free sends about 12,000 campaign emails a day. A bigger list pauses at the limit and carries on after midnight UTC, and a list over about 25,000 can't start. Bigger lists need Workers Paid, $5 a month, which you can turn on at any time." The README's "Workers Free or Paid" section in the checkout has the details.

Done when `bunx wrangler whoami` and `aws sts get-caller-identity` both succeed and you have every answer.

## 4. Deploy

Sendr keeps uploaded images and video in R2, which a Cloudflare account turns on once. Check with `bunx wrangler r2 bucket list`. If it fails saying R2 isn't enabled, ask the user to open R2 in the Cloudflare dashboard and turn it on; it may ask for a payment method, though the first 10 GB are free. Do this before the first deploy.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/ivryb/sendr.git
cd sendr
bun install
bunx wrangler queues create sendr-send
bunx react-router build && bunx wrangler deploy --domain emails.acme.com && bunx wrangler d1 migrations apply DB --remote
printf '%s' 'ann@acme.com' | bunx wrangler secret put ADMIN_EMAIL
```

The first deploy creates the D1 database and the R2 bucket. Without a Cloudflare domain, drop `--domain` and use the `workers.dev` address it prints. The domain stays attached, so later deploys are `bun run deploy`.

Each instance has its own checkout. The Worker, database, bucket and queue names in `wrangler.jsonc` are fixed, so a second instance in the same Cloudflare account would replace the first. Before deploying a second one, give it its own names: the Worker `name`, the D1 `database_name`, the R2 `bucket_name`, and the queue in both `producers` and `consumers` (for example `sendr-acme`, `sendr-acme`, `sendr-acme-media` and `sendr-acme-send`). Create that queue instead of `sendr-send`, and commit the change in the checkout so `git pull` merges later updates.

Campaign previews run a browser through Cloudflare Browser Run, which needs no setup. On the Workers Free plan it allows a new browser every 20 seconds and 10 browser-minutes a day, plenty for previews.

Done when `curl -s https://emails.acme.com/api/v1/docs` returns the API reference. A new custom domain can take a few minutes to get its certificate.

## 5. Give yourself an API key

From the checkout:

```sh
bun run api-key https://emails.acme.com --save
```

This creates a full-access key in the instance's database and saves it to `~/.config/sendr/emails.acme.com.env` as `SENDR_URL`, `SENDR_API_KEY` and `SENDR_CHECKOUT`. Your shell may not keep variables between commands, so load the file in every command that calls the API:

```sh
set -a; . ~/.config/sendr/emails.acme.com.env; set +a
curl -s "$SENDR_URL/api/v1/me" -H "Authorization: Bearer $SENDR_API_KEY"
```

Read `$SENDR_URL/api/v1/docs` now. It's the API reference for the rest of the setup. Then save the instance's address in settings with `PUT /settings` and `{ "publicUrl": "https://emails.acme.com" }`. Unsubscribe links and SES delivery reports use it.

Done when `GET /me` returns `"permissions":["full"]` and `GET /settings` returns the `publicUrl`.

## 6. Add the sender

1. Create an IAM user for this instance with the policy from the Senders section of the API reference, then an access key for it. Use `aws iam create-user`, `aws iam put-user-policy` and `aws iam create-access-key`. A new key takes about ten seconds to start working. Delete any policy file you wrote.
2. `POST /senders` with the name, address, region and the key.
3. `GET /senders/{id}` lists the DNS records SES needs. Add every one; on Cloudflare, set them to DNS only, not proxied. A domain can have only one DMARC record, so skip the `_dmarc` record if the domain already has one. Check the sender every few minutes until it's verified. That usually takes under an hour.

Done when `GET /senders/{id}` returns `"verified": true`.

## 7. Request SES production access

If the sender shows `"production": false`, the SES account is in its sandbox. It only sends to addresses verified in SES, so campaigns can't reach contacts yet. AWS grants production access on request, and it often denies vague requests. Read `docs/ses-production-access.md` in the checkout. Draft the request with the user, since it describes their business. Take the facts from them and show them the final text before you submit it with `aws sesv2 put-account-details`.

AWS usually answers within a day, so carry on without waiting. To test in the meantime, verify the user's own address with `aws sesv2 create-email-identity` and ask them to click the link AWS emails them.

Done when the request is submitted, or the sender already shows `"production": true`.

## 8. Send a test

Set the footer with `PUT /settings` (`footer` in Markdown, with the company name and postal address; Sendr adds the unsubscribe link below it). Create a short draft with `POST /campaigns` and show the user its picture from `GET /campaigns/{id}/screenshot` (the API reference says how). Then send it to them with `POST /campaigns/{id}/test`, and delete the draft after.

Done when the user confirms the test arrived and looks right.

## 9. Install the Sendr skill

Future sessions find Sendr through a `sendr` skill written for this project. It only points at the instance: the API reference at `/api/v1/docs` describes everything Sendr does and updates with every deploy, while a copied skill would not. Save it as `SKILL.md` in a `sendr` folder in the project's repository, where its skills live (`.claude/skills/` for Claude Code, `.agents/skills/` for Codex), so it travels with the project. Without a repository, save it in the user's skills directory (`~/.claude/skills/sendr/` or `~/.agents/skills/sendr/`).

Fill in the angle brackets from the user's answers in step 3, and keep the rest as written. The description is what makes later sessions reach for the skill, so keep its list of tasks. The skill holds no secrets.

```markdown
---
name: sendr
description: Email <Project>'s users through Sendr, its own email tool at <host>. Use for newsletters, campaigns, product updates and announcements; campaign results like opens, clicks and unsubscribes; single emails from the app, like welcome notes; syncing or importing contacts; and senders, the footer or updating Sendr.
---

# Sendr

<Project> sends its newsletters and campaigns through Sendr, its own email tool at <instance URL>, from <From address>.

Read <instance URL>/api/v1/docs at the start of each session. It's the reference for everything Sendr does, and it matches the deployed version.

Load `~/.config/sendr/<host>.env` (`SENDR_URL`, `SENDR_API_KEY`, `SENDR_CHECKOUT`) in every command that calls the API, since shell variables may not last between commands:

    set -a; . ~/.config/sendr/<host>.env; set +a

If the file is missing on this machine, run `bun run api-key <instance URL> --save` in a Sendr checkout.

Sends need <the user's name>'s go-ahead, as the API reference describes. Send tests to <their email>.
```

If the project sends other email elsewhere, like receipts from its app through another service, say so in a sentence after the first paragraph, so later sessions pick the right tool.

If the repository's `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md` lists its skills, add a line for `sendr` in the same style.

Done when the file is saved.

## 10. Hand over

Tell the user:

- Their Sendr address. They sign in there with their email and add a passkey. Until their own sender can email them, sendr.soy delivers the login code.
- What they can ask you now, for example: "draft this month's product update", "how did last week's campaign do?", "send a welcome email when someone signs up".
- How their app connects. Its backend needs a key with the contacts and emails permissions, which `bun run api-key https://emails.acme.com --name "Acme backend" --permissions contacts,emails` prints. With it, the app syncs each user with `PUT /contacts/{userId}` and sends single emails with `POST /emails`. Offer to wire this up in their app.
- What's still pending, like DNS verification or the SES production access request.
